    Track 2 · Hands-on · Lesson 3

    Build a tiny SFT dataset

    After this lesson you can build an SFT dataset as (prompt, completion) pairs, load real rows into a datasets.Dataset, deduplicate them, check class balance, make a stratified gold / train / validation split, and save the gold set to a file.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~9 min Prerequisites: Load a base model and tokenizer Verified: 13 Nov 2026

    The model is loaded; now it needs examples. We'll build a sentiment classification dataset from a small public source, so you see real rows, real duplicates and a real class balance, and so the training in Lesson 2.5 has enough steps to actually learn. Then we clean it, split it three ways and save the gold set to a file that Lesson 2.7 reads back.

    The shape: (prompt, completion)

    From Track 1: an SFT example is a prompt paired with the target completion. For classification the completion is just the label. Two hand-written rows show the shape:

    raw = [
    {"prompt": "Classify the sentiment as positive or negative: I loved this movie.", "completion": "positive"},
    {"prompt": "Classify the sentiment as positive or negative: It broke after one use.", "completion": "negative"},
]

    We keep the prompt instruction identical across examples so the model learns the task, not the wording. That is the right call when production always sends that exact prompt; if real users will phrase the request in different ways, vary the instruction in training too, or the model may only respond well to the one phrasing it saw.

    Load real rows into a datasets.Dataset

    The datasets library gives us a fast, memory-mapped table with .map(), .filter(), and splitting — the standard container the Trainer expects. Six hand-written rows would only prove the code runs: with Lesson 2.5's batch settings they make one optimizer step per epoch, and the model learns nothing you could measure. So we take 1,200 rows from rotten_tomatoes, a classic set of one-sentence movie-review snippets labelled positive or negative (about 1 MB to download).

    from datasets import load_dataset

INSTRUCTION = "Classify the sentiment as positive or negative: "
WORDS = {"neg": "negative", "pos": "positive"}

src = load_dataset("cornell-movie-review-data/rotten_tomatoes", split="train")   # 8,530 rows
names = src.features["label"].names          # ['neg', 'pos']

def to_pair(row):
    return {"prompt": INSTRUCTION + row["text"],
            "completion": WORDS[names[row["label"]]]}

ds = src.shuffle(seed=42).select(range(1200)).map(to_pair, remove_columns=["text"])
print(ds)       # columns: label, prompt, completion (label is kept for the stratified split)
print(ds[0])

    The dataset card lists the licence as unknown: it is Pang and Lee's 2005 research release. That is fine for learning; check the terms before you build anything you ship on it. With your own data, Dataset.from_list(raw) or load_dataset("json", data_files="rows.jsonl") gives you the same kind of table.

    Deduplicate

    Track 1 told you to remove duplicates; here is the code. Normalise each prompt (lower case, collapse whitespace), keep the first row for each normalised prompt, and drop the rest. Exact duplicates waste steps and, worse, can land on both sides of a split, which inflates every score you measure later.

    def norm(text):
    return " ".join(text.lower().split())

first = {}
for i, prompt in enumerate(ds["prompt"]):
    first.setdefault(norm(prompt), i)      # index of the first row with this prompt
print(len(ds) - len(first), "duplicate prompts dropped")   # 0 for this sample; see the try-it
ds = ds.select(sorted(first.values()))

    This only catches exact duplicates after normalisation. Near-duplicates (the same review with one word changed) need fuzzy matching (MinHash is a common choice); Lesson 1.7 explains why they matter.

    Check class balance

    Track 1 warned that imbalance lets a model cheat. Check it in one line:

    from collections import Counter
print(Counter(ds["completion"]))   # Counter({'negative': 610, 'positive': 590})

    Apply what you learned

    Before training, also confirm the labels are correct (read 20 random rows; public datasets carry label noise too) and make sure the examples resemble the inputs you'll really see. Garbage in, garbage out — the data lessons of Track 1 are where most of your quality comes from.

    Split three ways: gold, train, validation

    We need three disjoint sets. A gold set (Lesson 1.8) that you never train on and never use to pick a checkpoint; Lesson 2.7 judges the fine-tune on it. A validation slice to watch for overfitting during training. And the training rows. Cut the gold set first, then split the rest. stratify_by_column keeps the positive/negative ratio the same in every part, which a random cut only does on average; it needs a class-label column, which is why we kept label.

    cut = ds.train_test_split(test_size=200, stratify_by_column="label", seed=42)
gold_ds = cut["test"]                                  # 200 rows, never trained on
rest = cut["train"].train_test_split(test_size=0.1, stratify_by_column="label", seed=42)
train_ds, val_ds = rest["train"], rest["test"]
print(len(train_ds), "train /", len(val_ds), "val /", len(gold_ds), "gold")   # 900 train / 100 val / 200 gold

# save the gold set as a file: Lesson 2.7 reads it back
gold_ds.select_columns(["prompt", "completion"]) \
       .rename_column("completion", "label") \
       .to_json("gold.jsonl")                          # one JSON object per line

    Open gold.jsonl and read it before you rely on it. A gold set is supposed to be hand-checked: fix or drop any row whose label you disagree with, and keep the file fixed from now on so that scores from different runs stay comparable. With data in hand, the next step is turning these strings into the token tensors the model consumes.

    Key idea

    Data work is the real work. A Dataset of clean, deduplicated, balanced, representative (prompt, completion) pairs — plus a gold set saved to a file and never trained on — is what makes the rest of the pipeline meaningful.

    Recap

    • An SFT row is a (prompt, completion) pair; for classification the completion is the label.
    • Deduplicate on normalised prompts and check class balance before you split.
    • Cut the gold set first, then train and validation, all stratified; save gold.jsonl, hand-check it and never train on it.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    Prove the dedup step works. Append a copy of the first row with its prompt upper-cased and padded with spaces, then rerun the dedup cell: from datasets import concatenate_datasets, dup = ds.select([0]).map(lambda r: {"prompt": " " + r["prompt"].upper() + " "}), ds = concatenate_datasets([ds, dup]). How many rows does it drop? Would it still catch the copy without norm()?

    Show answer

    It drops 1 row: norm() lower-cases and collapses whitespace, so the copy maps to the same key as row 0. Without norm() the two strings differ and both stay, and if they land on different sides of a split, the gold score is inflated by a row the model trained on. (The 1,200 rows drawn here have no exact duplicates of their own; real merged or scraped data usually does.)

    Key terms

    datasets.Dataset
    A fast, memory-mapped table with map/filter/split that the Trainer consumes.
    from_list
    Builds a Dataset from a list of dicts.
    class balance
    Keeping labels roughly even so accuracy reflects real skill.
    train_test_split
    Splits a Dataset into train and held-out portions.
    gold set
    A small, never-trained-on set with verified answers, used to judge quality.
